case_study_insert.main_stem: Quayline West Transit (QWT) is a public limited company in the regional bus and coach transport sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 1998 by Priya Raman, it runs services along the western coast and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. QWT plans to invest $900,000 in a fleet of electric buses and charging depots, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $18, and currently produces 70,000 units a year, each unit one paying passenger journey. QWT faces rising labour turnover among drivers and a defect rate of 3.5% in vehicle maintenance checks.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The western network ran 18,000 bus services last quarter with a maintenance defect rate of 3.5%, down from 5.2% a year earlier. Passenger complaints fell from 62 to 34 per month. Average punctuality is 88.0% of services running on time. A survey of 700 commuters found that 61% would switch to electric buses if fares stayed the same, and 49% cite reliability as the main reason for choosing QWT. A driver audit shows 22 of 70 drivers need retraining on electric vehicle systems; certification courses cost $650 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Quayline West Transit for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.8%, increasing the cost of QWT's $600,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.50 to $13.25 per hour from April 2026, raising the wage bill for its 70 drivers and staff. (3) Diesel and electricity costs for the fleet have risen 11.0% year-on-year, while passenger fare revenue grew only 2.0% and regional bus usage fell 1.5%.

questions.question_text: QWT financed its $900,000 electric bus fleet with a $600,000 bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for QWT of using the share issue rather than more bank borrowing for this expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $300,000 raised by a share issue does not have to be repaid and carries no interest, so it eases the cash flow burden on QWT, which already pays interest on a $600,000 bank loan and bears fixed costs of $450,000 a year. That saving helps hold the $18 fare steady while fleet energy costs rise, keeping the service attractive to the 61% of surveyed commuters who would switch to electric buses.

Point 2: Equity strengthens QWT's balance sheet because the $300,000 increases capital Employed without adding a creditor who could demand repayment or seize buses if passenger revenue falls. As a public limited company, QWT can issue shares to existing holders or new investors, preserving borrowing capacity for the charging depots and allowing founder Priya Raman to keep the $900,000 project on schedule despite rising labour turnover among drivers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to QWT, its legal structure and its financing mix.

questions.question_text: QWT is launching its new electric bus services. Consider local radio advertising, social media campaigns, or digital displays at bus stations. Which should QWT choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Local radio is relatively cheap and can repeatedly reach the western-coast communities QWT actually serves, making it good for a time-limited launch message about electric buses. Its limitation is that it cannot show the buses or convey reliability, which the survey shows matters to 49% of the 700 commuters, and its audience is broad rather than made up of regular passengers.

Social media campaigns: Short videos and targeted posts can demonstrate the quiet electric buses and the 88.0% punctuality record directly to commuters, with measurable engagement at low cost. Posts can highlight that 61% of surveyed commuters would switch to electric buses if fares stayed the same. The drawback is that older or occasional travellers may not be reached, and online attention is fleeting compared with a 18,000-service-a-quarter operation that needs steady daily ridership.

Digital displays at bus stations: Screens at QWT's own stops reach passengers exactly at the point of purchase, can show live reliability and route information, and directly address the 49% who choose QWT for reliability. Installation and content costs are higher than radio and the audience is limited to people already using the network, so it does little to attract the 61% who might switch from other modes.

Recommendation: QWT should choose digital displays at bus stations, backed by low-cost social media. Station displays reach the real riders at the decision moment and can demonstrate the punctuality that 49% value, while social media extends the message to the 61% who would switch. Local radio is rejected because it is untargeted and cannot show the new buses; social media alone is rejected because it misses station-based passengers, and station displays alone would not win new commuters.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to QWT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of QWT with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of QWT with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and social media alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: QWT has democratic leadership but rising labour turnover among its drivers and 22 needing electric-vehicle retraining. Explain two benefits for QWT of using democratic leadership to improve staff motivation and retention.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 70 drivers a voice in how the new electric bus routes and charging schedules are organised, satisfying social and esteem needs and increasing job satisfaction. Drivers who help shape their own rotas are more likely to stay, directly tackling the rising labour turnover and protecting the 18,000 services QWT runs each quarter.

Point 2: Involving drivers in decisions generates practical feedback from the people who handle the buses daily, helping reduce the 3.5% maintenance defect rate as the fleet changes. Higher involvement lowers the chances that the 22 drivers needing retraining feel alienated, so the $650 certification courses are more likely to succeed and punctuality can be protected at 88.0% while the $900,000 fleet investment beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to QWT's leadership style, labour turnover and maintenance quality.

questions.question_text: QWT must retrain 22 drivers on the new electric vehicles. Consider on-the-job training or external certification courses at $650 per driver. Which should QWT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training on QWT's own electric buses keeps the 22 drivers productive and learning routes while they train, avoiding course fees and protecting the 18,000 services run each quarter. It is tailored to QWT's actual charging procedures and helps address the 3.5% defect rate immediately. However, trainer-drivers lose time from their duties, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no formal certificate, which may matter when 49% of surveyed commuters rate reliability as their reason for choosing QWT.

External certification courses at $650 per driver: These provide structured, up-to-date electric-vehicle skills and a recognised qualification for all 22 drivers (22 × $650 = $14,300), a cost that is small next to the $900,000 fleet investment. They take drivers off the road temporarily, reducing capacity, and the generic syllabus may not cover QWT's specific depot routines, so follow-up on site would still be needed.

Decision: QWT should choose external certification for the 22 drivers, followed by short on-the-job induction at the depot. Certification is chosen because the $14,300 cost is modest, a formal qualification supports the reliability that 49% of commuters demand, and electric vehicles are a fundamentally new technology that cannot be learned safely by imitation alone. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it would pass on habits linked to the 5.2% defect rate of a year ago and leave no evidence of competence for a public limited company managing a $600,000 loan-funded fleet.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to QWT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of QWT.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of QWT with a well-justified decision covering cost, reliability and new-technology competence.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how QWT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $450,000 ÷ ($18 − $9) = $450,000 ÷ $9 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 passenger journeys a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $18 − $9 = $9. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways QWT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. QWT can compare the 50,000-journey break-even with 70,000 journeys actually sold, a margin of safety of 20,000 journeys, to assess whether the $900,000 electric fleet is justified.
2. Contribution of $9 per journey lets managers test a fare freeze or discount: holding the $18 fare protects contribution as 11.0% energy costs rise, and the effect of a $1 fare cut can be modelled before it is offered.
3. Fixed costs of $450,000 and $9 contribution set the minimum 50,000 journeys needed to cover costs and service the $600,000 bank loan.
4. Labour productivity of 70,000 units ÷ 70 staff = 1,000 journeys per worker can be tracked to judge whether the 22 retrained drivers and falling 3.5% defect rate are improving efficiency.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 70,000 journeys; fare-freeze modelling at $18; loan-service volume for the $600,000 debt; and productivity benchmarking at 1,000 journeys per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QWT's profitability using the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has QWT's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue increased from $1,800,000 to $2,100,000 while cost of sales rose from $1,080,000 to $1,176,000; gross profit therefore rose from $720,000 to $924,000. Dividing gross profit by revenue gives 40.0% in 2024 and 44.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $216,000 on $1,800,000 and $315,000 on $2,100,000 produces 12.0% and 15.0%. Operating profit against capital employed of $1,200,000 and $1,500,000 gives 18.0% and 21.0%.

Evaluation: Profitability strengthened on every measure. The gross margin rising from 40.0% to 44.0% shows QWT retained more of each fare after direct operating costs, consistent with the $9 contribution on each of 70,000 journeys. The operating margin improving from 12.0% to 15.0% indicates the $450,000 fixed costs were spread over more passengers. Returns on the growing capital base rose from 18.0% to 21.0%, so the $900,000 electric fleet appears to be adding value. However, interest payable rose from $24,000 to $30,000 as the $600,000 loan takes effect, and if regional bus usage keeps falling 1.5% the extra passengers needed to sustain these margins may not arrive.

Conclusion: QWT's financial performance has improved. All three margins rose together and the improvement is not just a revenue effect, since costs rose more slowly than revenue. The residual concern is the rising interest charge and soft demand, so QWT should protect the gains by keeping fares competitive and monitoring ridership as the electric fleet expands.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether QWT's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QWT of replacing diesel buses with the new electric buses.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Electric buses cut exhaust emissions and support QWT's sustainability credentials, which matters because 61% of the 700 surveyed commuters said they would switch to electric buses if fares stayed the same. This can win new riders, protect the $18 fare and help justify the $900,000 fleet investment, while also reducing exposure to the 11.0% rise in diesel costs reported in Appendix 3.

Disadvantage: The switch requires expensive charging depots within the $900,000 budget and new skills for the 22 drivers needing retraining at $650 each, adding cost and disruption. Electric range and charging time could reduce service flexibility across a wide western-coast network, threatening the 88.0% punctuality record that 49% of commuters rate as their main reason for choosing QWT, especially while labour turnover among drivers is rising.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to QWT's survey data, costs and service reliability.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.8%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.0% rise in fleet energy costs will affect QWT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.8%): If QWT's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the increase is 0.8 percentage points (4.8% − 4.0%), so extra annual interest is 0.8% × $600,000 = $4,800 a year. That is modest against fixed costs of $450,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is nil. The larger risk is indirect: higher rates may suppress consumer spending, but QWT can hedge by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.25 per hour): With a workforce of 70, driving and depot roles are largely hourly-paid, so the rise lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so a total wage cost cannot be honestly invented; the defensible test is productivity of 70,000 journeys ÷ 70 staff = 1,000 journeys per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if labour turnover pushes it down, the $9 contribution per journey is squeezed.

Fleet energy costs (11.0% rise in diesel and electricity): These feed into the $9 variable cost on each of 70,000 journeys. The insert does not split that cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $9 were energy and it rose 11.0%, that would be 11.0% × $9 = $0.99 per journey, or up to $69,300 a year at 70,000 journeys — but energy is only part of variable cost, so the true figure is lower and cannot be stated exactly from the insert. Because fares grew only 2.0% and usage fell 1.5%, QWT cannot easily pass this on.

Conclusion: The 11.0% rise in fleet energy costs will have the greatest impact. It touches every journey, far exceeds the $4,800 interest effect, and is harder to offset than wages because fares are growing only 2.0% while demand is falling. The interest rise is the smallest and can be fixed; the wage rise is significant but manageable at 1,000 journeys per worker. Energy inflation directly erodes the $9 contribution that underpins the $900,000 fleet investment, so it matters most.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to QWT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on QWT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of QWT with a well-justified judgment that fleet energy inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
